lessons.plainEnglish: Alcohol takes away the three things driving depends on: staying alert, judging situations correctly, and seeing clearly. It does not hit everyone the same way, or even hit the same person the same way twice — your mood, tiredness, other medication and how much you have eaten all change the effect. And there is no trick that speeds up sobering up. Coffee and a cold shower make a drunk person a wide-awake drunk person, nothing more. Only time lowers blood alcohol.
lessons.whyItMatters: People get caught out by two beliefs: that they can tell how drunk they are, and that they can sober up quickly if they need to. Both are wrong, and the handbook says so directly. Judgment is one of the first things alcohol damages — which means the part of you deciding whether you are fine to drive is the part already affected.
lessons.example: You have three beers over two hours at a friend's house, then drink a large coffee and stand outside in the cold for twenty minutes because you want to drive home. Your blood alcohol has not dropped at all. Worse, because BAC keeps climbing after the last drink, you may be more impaired pulling out of the driveway than you were in the kitchen.

lessons.plainEnglish: West Virginia treats drivers under 21 completely differently from adults. For an adult, the question is whether BAC reached 0.08. For someone under 21, there is no threshold to argue about — any measurable alcohol costs you your licence. Separately, simply by driving on West Virginia roads you have already agreed to take a breath test if you are arrested for DUI. Refusing is not a way out: it carries its own revocation of one year up to life, on top of whatever the DUI charge does.
lessons.whyItMatters: Two traps live here. The first is thinking 0.08 is a safe line to drive up to — a licence can be revoked below 0.08, and between 0.05 and 0.08 the state can use that reading as evidence of impairment. The second is thinking refusing the test protects you. It does the opposite, and the handbook explains why the law exists: the test protects the driver who has not been drinking by giving a medically accepted measurement.
lessons.example: A 19-year-old has one beer at a party and drives home an hour later. An adult with that same BAC might be under every threshold. The 19-year-old is not — any measurable alcohol under 21 means losing the licence, regardless of how fine they feel or how well they drove.

lessons.plainEnglish: A prescription from a doctor is not permission to drive impaired. Plenty of ordinary medicines — allergy tablets, cold medicine, painkillers, sleep aids — cause exactly the drowsiness and loss of coordination that make driving dangerous, and mixing them with alcohol is worse than either alone. Being badly short of sleep does the same thing without any substance involved at all.
lessons.whyItMatters: People who would never drive after drinking will happily drive after a double dose of cold medicine or a 20-hour day. The handbook puts these in the same chapter as alcohol on purpose: the effect on your reaction time and judgment is comparable, and so is the crash risk.
lessons.example: You take an over-the-counter antihistamine for a bad cold before an evening drive. It is legal, it was recommended on the box, and you feel only slightly foggy. That fogginess is slowed reaction time — the same thing you would be criticised for if it came from a beer.

questions.question: According to the handbook, what does alcohol do to a driver?
choices: Reduces alertness, interferes with judgment, and impairs vision
Affects reaction time only, leaving judgment intact
Impairs vision only after the legal limit is reached
Slows the body but sharpens concentration
questions.explanation: The handbook lists three effects together: alcohol reduces alertness, interferes with judgment, and impairs vision. Judgment is included deliberately — the ability you would use to decide whether you are safe to drive is itself damaged, which is why self-assessment after drinking is unreliable.

questions.question: A driver says he can tell he is still fine to drive because he feels alert. Why is that reasoning unreliable?
choices: Alcohol interferes with judgment, so the ability he is using to assess himself is already affected
Feeling alert is a reliable sign, but only below 0.08 BAC
Alertness is unaffected by alcohol; only vision is impaired
It is reliable as long as he has eaten recently
questions.explanation: The handbook lists interference with judgment as one of alcohol's effects. Self-assessment depends on judgment, so a drinking driver is using an impaired faculty to decide whether he is impaired. Food and feeling alert change how drunk someone feels, not their blood alcohol.

questions.question: What is the only thing that sobers a person up?
choices: Time
Black coffee
A cold shower
Fresh air and exercise
questions.explanation: The handbook names black coffee, fresh air, cold showers, physical exercise and other home remedies specifically, and says they do not effectively help someone sober up. Time is the only sobering influence. Those remedies can make a person feel more awake while their blood alcohol is unchanged, which is more dangerous, not less.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an effective way to sober someone up before driving?
choices: All of these are ineffective: coffee, a cold shower, and fresh air
Waiting several hours
Not drinking in the first place
Arranging a designated driver
questions.explanation: Coffee, cold showers, fresh air and exercise are all named in the handbook as home remedies that do not work. Waiting works because time is the only sobering influence, and not drinking or using a designated driver avoids the problem entirely.

questions.question: What happens to blood alcohol concentration when someone has more than one drink per hour?
choices: It builds up in the body and can keep rising after the last drink
It levels off automatically after the second drink
It falls steadily as soon as drinking stops
It stays constant until the body has processed all food
questions.explanation: The handbook explains that BAC builds up when drinks come faster than one per hour, and gives an example where BAC is still above 0.06 percent at 4 a.m. after a last drink at 11:30 p.m. This is why someone can be more impaired later than when they stopped drinking.

questions.question: A driver has her last drink at 11:30 p.m. and sleeps for a few hours. Why might she still be arrested for DUI at 4 a.m.?
choices: BAC continues to build after the last drink and can still be above 0.06 percent hours later
Sleeping prevents the body from processing alcohol at all
A DUI arrest can only occur within one hour of drinking
BAC doubles overnight regardless of how much was drunk
questions.explanation: This is the handbook's own worked example: with a last drink at 11:30 p.m., BAC keeps increasing and is still above 0.06 percent at 4 a.m. Someone at that level can be arrested for DUI. Sleeping a few hours is not the same as being sober.

questions.question: Which statement about how alcohol affects people is correct?
choices: It affects a person differently at different times, depending on physical and emotional condition, other drugs and food
It affects everyone identically for a given body weight
It has no effect until the third drink
Its effect depends only on the type of drink consumed
questions.explanation: The handbook says alcohol affects a person differently at different times, and names physical and emotional conditions, other drugs, and even the amount of food in the stomach as things that change the effect. That variability is why a personal rule like 'two drinks is fine for me' is unreliable.

questions.question: A driver knows from experience that two drinks never affects him. Tonight he is tired, has eaten nothing, and is taking cold medicine. What does the handbook suggest?
choices: Alcohol can affect him differently tonight because condition, other drugs and food all change its effect
His past experience is a reliable guide regardless of conditions
Cold medicine cancels out the effect of two drinks
An empty stomach reduces the effect of alcohol
questions.explanation: The handbook names exactly these factors — physical and emotional conditions, other drugs, and the amount of food in the stomach — as reasons alcohol has a varied effect. It also warns separately that alcohol and drugs together can be a deadly combination. Past experience under different conditions proves nothing about tonight.

choices: They will lose their driver's license
They receive a warning for a first occurrence
Nothing, provided their BAC is under 0.08
They are fined but keep their license
questions.explanation: West Virginia has a zero tolerance law for drivers under 21. The handbook states that if any amount of alcohol is found in the system of a driver under 21, that driver will lose their license. The adult 0.08 threshold does not apply to them.

The presumption applies only if they are under 21
questions.explanation: At 0.08 percent or more the handbook says the driver is presumed to be driving under the influence, so 0.09 is over that line. The weaker 'relevant evidence' wording applies to readings above 0.05 but below 0.08, and the zero tolerance rule is a separate, stricter rule for drivers under 21.

questions.question: Can a West Virginia driver's license be revoked if their BAC is below 0.08 percent?
choices: Yes — the handbook states a license can be revoked with a BAC less than 0.08 percent
No — 0.08 is an absolute floor for any penalty
Only if the driver is also speeding
Only for commercial drivers
questions.explanation: The handbook says plainly that under West Virginia law your driver's license can be revoked if your BAC is less than 0.08 percent. It also states that a BAC above 0.05 and below 0.08 is relevant evidence to presume impaired driving. Treating 0.08 as a safe limit to drive up to is a mistake.

choices: Relevant evidence to presume the driver's ability to drive is impaired
Conclusive proof of driving under the influence
Legally irrelevant
Grounds for a fine but never a revocation
questions.explanation: The handbook uses precise wording: between 0.05 and 0.08 the reading is relevant evidence to presume impaired ability to drive. That is weaker than the 0.08 presumption of driving under the influence, but it is far from irrelevant, and revocation below 0.08 is possible.

questions.question: What is the consequence of refusing the Breathalyzer after a DUI arrest in West Virginia?
choices: Your privilege to operate a motor vehicle is revoked for one year and up to life
Nothing, since the test is voluntary
A fine, but your license is unaffected
A 30-day suspension only
questions.explanation: Under the Implied Consent Law you are deemed to have already consented to the test by driving. The handbook states that refusing revokes your privilege to operate a motor vehicle for a period of one year and up to life. Refusal is not a way to avoid consequences.

questions.question: A driver arrested for DUI refuses the breath test, believing that without a reading there is no evidence. Is that reasoning sound?
choices: No — refusal itself carries a revocation of one year up to life
Yes — without a BAC reading no penalty can follow
Yes, provided the driver requests a blood test instead within 24 hours
No, but only because refusal adds a fine
questions.explanation: Consent is implied by the act of driving, so refusing is itself a violation carrying revocation of one year up to life — separate from the DUI charge. The handbook also notes the law protects drivers who have not been drinking, since the test gives a medically accepted measurement.

choices: A prescribed Safety and Treatment program
A defensive driving course only
A second road skills test only
Nothing — the license returns automatically when the period ends
questions.explanation: The handbook states that any time a license is revoked or suspended for a DUI, a prescribed Safety and Treatment program must be completed before becoming eligible to reinstate driving privileges. Simply waiting out the revocation period is not enough.

questions.explanation: Reinstatement is not automatic. It reports the driver's location to the DMV continuously
It limits the vehicle's top speed after a DUI
It replaces the requirement for a driver's license
questions.explanation: The handbook describes the Interlock device as attaching to the ignition system of a vehicle and preventing an intoxicated person from starting the car. The Interlock Program lets a person drive legally provided they operate a vehicle fitted with the device.

For every first offense without exception
Only for drivers over the age of 21
Only when a crash caused injury

questions.question: What is the legal drinking age in West Virginia?
questions.explanation: The handbook states the legal drinking age in West Virginia is 21 years old. This is the age that also defines who falls under the zero tolerance law for driving with any measurable alcohol.

choices: Under 21 — the same as the legal drinking age
Under 18 — the age of majority
Under 25 — the age used for insurance purposes
Under 16 — the minimum licensing age
questions.explanation: The zero tolerance law applies to drivers under the age of 21, matching the legal drinking age of 21. A driver under 21 with any measurable alcohol loses their license regardless of whether they reach the adult 0.08 threshold.

Only illegal drugs
Only drugs taken together with alcohol
Only drugs that carry a written warning label
questions.explanation: The handbook says that using drugs, even if prescribed by a physician or bought over the counter, can cause drowsiness, loss of coordination, hallucinations or total body malfunctions. A legal prescription does not make you safe to drive.

Cold medicine offsets the effects of a single beer
Over-the-counter medicines have no effect on driving
The combination is safe as long as BAC stays under 0.08

About 36 hours
About 10 hours
questions.explanation: The handbook states that after being awake for 18 hours, with some variation, driving skills are comparable to someone under the influence of drugs or alcohol. Drowsy driving decreases reaction time and increases crash risk, which is why it appears in the impairment chapter.

questions.question: You have been awake since 5 a.m. and it is now nearly midnight. You have had nothing to drink. How should you treat your fitness to drive?
choices: As impaired — after about 18 hours awake, driving skills are comparable to being under the influence
As completely unimpaired, since no alcohol or drugs are involved
As impaired only if you actually fall asleep at the wheel
As safe, because tiredness affects comfort rather than reaction time
questions.explanation: That is roughly 19 hours awake. The handbook puts drowsy driving in the impairment chapter precisely because the effect is comparable: slower reaction time and increased crash risk, often with too little time to brake or steer away. No alcohol is needed to be dangerously impaired.
